source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design (ICLR 2026)
finding: Picking each question by expected information gain (EIG) over sampled hypotheses roughly doubles 20 Questions success versus asking the model directly.
numbers: Average +37.4 percentage points over Prompt-Only across 6 LLMs and 3 target sets; never decreased. Table 1 (100 targets per set): Animals GPT-4o-mini 44% -> 88%; Celebrities Mistral-Large 19% -> 91%; Things GPT-4o 34% -> 64%.
quote: On average, BED-LLM improves the success rate by 37.4 percentage points compared to direct prompting
limits: Answerer is an LLM, not a human. Hypotheses are sampled by the same LLM. 20 turns max.
agent_relevance: Strong support for S7 'pick the discriminating test by computing it in code'. The gain comes from code-side scoring, not model judgment.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM (ICLR 2026)
finding: A simple half-split baseline (Split: choose the question that splits sampled hypotheses most evenly) already recovers most of the gain; full EIG adds more on top.
numbers: Animals Qwen2.5-72B: Prompt-Only 45, Split 87, BED-LLM 95. Celebrities GPT-4o: 45 / 63 / 86. Things Llama-3.3-70B: 34 / 46 / 55.
limits: Split equals marginal-entropy maximisation only when the answer is deterministic given the hypothesis. Authors say their Split is far stronger than earlier reports.
agent_relevance: Half-split is the cheap special case and gets about two thirds of the benefit. Start there; add a noisy-answer likelihood only if tests are noisy.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM (ICLR 2026)
finding: Asking the model to pick the best question itself (Implicit Maximization, same candidate questions as BED-LLM) is much worse than computing EIG.
numbers: Animals: Mistral-Large Implicit 53 vs BED-LLM 95; GPT-4o 70 vs 93. Things GPT-4o-mini 25 vs 49.
quote: passing the samples to an LLM and prompting it to select the highest-EIG question ... works much less well
limits: Gap varies by model.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G5: code selects. A model told to pick the most informative probe loses most of the benefit.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM (ICLR 2026)
finding: Chain-of-thought about which question helps most does not close the gap. Rough ordering: Prompt-Only < CoT < Split < Entropy < full EIG.
numbers: Animals GPT-4o: Prompt-Only 45, CoT 62, BED-LLM 93. Things Mistral-Large: 26, 29, 58. Llama-3.3-70B Animals: CoT 40 equals Prompt-Only 40.
limits: One CoT prompt design (ReAct-style) only.
agent_relevance: Reasoning prose about what to test is a weak substitute for computing the split.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM (ICLR 2026)
finding: How beliefs are formed matters a lot. Raw in-context beliefs (no filtering of hypotheses against the history) collapse performance. Uncertainty must be measured over answers, not over hypotheses.
numbers: ICL Beliefs: Animals GPT-4o-mini 18% vs BED-LLM 88%; Celebrities GPT-4o 52 vs 86. Data-Estimation pairing worse than prior-likelihood: Animals Llama-3.3-70B 40 vs 79; Mistral Celebrities 66 vs 91.
limits: Ablations on 20 Questions only.
agent_relevance: The candidate set must be re-filtered by code against all outcomes seen so far (matches G2/G3). Never let the model carry the survivor set in its head.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM (ICLR 2026)
finding: On a softer task (inferring a user's film taste, 5 questions, 200 profiles) the gain is small, and Prompt-Only is a stronger baseline there.
numbers: Mean rating of 10 recommendations (1-5 scale): BED-LLM above Prompt-Only and Entropy, most clear when questioner and answerer are different models. Exact deltas only in plots.
limits: Judged by an LLM; no human users. Abstract target, no clear hypothesis set.
agent_relevance: EIG probing pays most when hypotheses are concrete and tests have crisp outcomes (code, ARC rule candidates), less for open-ended goals.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM (ICLR 2026)
finding: Benefit holds when the answerer is a different model from the questioner, and the relative gain is largest for the weakest model.
numbers: Mismatch setups (GPT-4o-mini asks / Qwen2.5-72B answers, and reverse): Animals about 90 for BED-LLM. Llama-3.1-8B: Animals 8 -> 63, Celebrities 10 -> 58, Things 10 -> 26.
limits: Small 8B model still low in absolute terms on Things.
agent_relevance: Scaffold helps small models most; consistent with G12 (spend by difficulty).

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions: Enhancing LLMs with Preference Optimization and Expected Information Gain
finding: Training Llama-2-chat 7B with DPO on pairs of low-EIG vs high-EIG questions makes it ask more informative questions and win more 20 Questions games, also in other domains.
numbers: Zero-shot vs DPO success: INLG 56.7% vs 68.9%; Things 51.1% vs 61.1%; Celebrities 71.1% vs 72.2%; mean EIG 0.34->0.45, 0.29->0.40, 0.35->0.47. Plain fine-tuning on INLG got 46.6%, below zero-shot. Out-of-domain BigBench: 17.2% vs 31.0%.
limits: Test sets are small (about 45 games each). One 7B model. EIG computed over a closed item set.
agent_relevance: EIG is a usable signal to rank candidate probes. Plain imitation did not teach probing; the EIG contrast did.

source: Mazzaccara et al. (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions
finding: Open-ended and abstract targets are much harder than concrete items, and EIG needs a closed candidate set.
numbers: Concrete targets 25.0% -> 37.5% with DPO; abstract targets 7.7% -> 23.1%. Abstract-target EIG fell (0.29 -> 0.24).
limits: Authors note EIG in an open set needs candidates from outside sources. Tiny sample (13 targets in the abstract group).
agent_relevance: Boundary: if the hypothesis set is not enumerated, EIG is not defined. Our S2 must produce explicit candidate rules before S7 can score probes.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose Lips Sink Ships: Asking Questions in Battleship with Language-Informed Program Sampling (CogSci 2024)
finding: Sample questions from an LLM, turn each into a program, compute its EIG on the board, keep the best. A few samples reach human-average informativeness.
numbers: 18 boards, human N=40, 605 question-board pairs: mean human EIG 1.27 bits, best human 3.61. One-shot LLM samples (k=1): EIG about 0.65-0.66; hand grammar 0.36. At k=5 both LLMs near human mean; at k=10 both beat it (p<0.001 CodeLlama, p=0.01 GPT-4). Never reached the top 10-20% of humans.
limits: Single-turn Battleship; questions must fit a domain language; only 40-88% of LLM questions translate to valid programs.
agent_relevance: Generate-many-then-score-by-EIG is the cheap loop: 5-10 candidate probes is enough. Quality ceiling is below the best human.

source: Grand et al. (2024) Loose Lips Sink Ships
finding: LLMs asked directly often ask redundant questions, and GPT-4V did not use the board image.
numbers: 40% (CodeLlama) and 33% (GPT-4) of valid questions had EIG=0 (redundant with what the board already showed). Visual board no better than no-board for k=10-50 and significantly worse at k=1 and 5 (p<0.05). Only the textual grid beat no-board.
quote: GPT-4V was unable to utilize the board's structure to formulate informative questions
limits: One model family and one task. Zero-shot GPT-4 translated to valid programs only 40% of the time.
agent_relevance: Failure mode: probes that repeat known information. Code must check each probe splits the current survivor set (EIG>0) before it is run (G2).

source: Kriz, Berthon, Astorga, van der Schaar (2026) Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs
finding: On reasoning models, inference-time BED-LLM gave only modest gains over the base model and was sometimes worse, at about 61x the time.
numbers: Eval time per game: BED-LLM 2376 s vs trained AR-BED 38.9 s (61.1x). BED-LLM worse than the non-reasoning base on some domains in both solve rate and EIG. Domains: animals, plants, countries, celebrities.
limits: Authors' own reimplementation of BED-LLM; their method uses an external generative model. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Tension with c01: the EIG loop's gain depends on how good the LLM-built answer model is. Cost matters (G7): log token cost of the probe loop.

source: Kriz et al. (2026) Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs
finding: Information-gathering training on Twenty Questions transfers to simulated clinical questioning.
numbers: MediQ-style, 5 questions, GPT-5 patient. Held-out dermatology (n=95): accuracy 90.5 -> 94.7%. Other specialties (n=92): 84.8 -> 90.2%. Correct-answer likelihood 76.0 -> 79.2 and 72.8 -> 78.1; Brier 0.165 -> 0.120 (derm).
limits: Simulated patients; synthetic 50-disease contrastive sets; SEM about 2-4 points so some gains are within noise.
agent_relevance: Probing skill can be general, but this needed training; we only have scaffolds.

source: Kriz et al. (2026) Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs
finding: Looking more than one test ahead (non-myopic EIG) gives only small gains in open questioning, but clear gains where a test is useless alone and useful later.
numbers: Cube-NM style task: two-step policy substantially beats one-step. In Twenty Questions, K=2 and K=3 lookahead give some gains at 2- and 3-question horizons; immediate and downstream EIG rankings can differ.
limits: Exact numbers are in the appendix, not read.
agent_relevance: Greedy one-step EIG is a good default (G11). Add lookahead only where a test pays off in combination.

source: Hartmann et al. (2026) Amortising Bayesian Experimental Design for Sequential Information Gathering in LLMs (ASIG, ICML 2026 workshop)
finding: RL fine-tuning with an EIG reward more than doubles a 7B model's 20 Questions success and runs 25-36x faster than BED-LLM.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B: more than doubles baseline success and beats BED-LLM on animals. Qwen2.5-14B: only +4.2 (animals) and +1.8 (plants) points; BED-LLM better on 14B plants but far below base on animals. 5 episodes.
quote: BED-LLM achieves the highest overall rate, but this is partly driven by hard-coded guessing logic
limits: Workshop paper, non-archival. BED-LLM's top score is partly from hard-coded guessing when fewer than 3 candidates remain.
agent_relevance: The 'guess when the set is small' rule is worth a lot; keep it in code.

source: Hartmann et al. (2026) ASIG
finding: Transfer of the learned probing to medical questioning (MediQ) is weak.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B accuracy 46.7 -> 47.6 (+0.9), voluntary accuracy 50.1 -> 51.8, overconfidence 36.1 -> 33.4%. Qwen2.5-14B accuracy 54.1 -> 54.2, voluntary accuracy 64.6 -> 63.0.
limits: Differences of 1-2 points are likely within noise; no CIs given.
agent_relevance: Do not expect probing gains to transfer for free to a new domain.

source: Kesmen et al. (2026) MoBayes: A Modular Bayesian Framework for Separating Reasoning from Language in Conversational Clinical Decision Support
finding: An LLM that only parses answers, with code doing the Bayes update, EIG question choice and stopping, beats frontier LLMs doing it all themselves.
numbers: DDxPlus (PatientSim), n=50 per cell. MoBayes + GPT-5.4-nano: top-1 78%, selective accuracy 81.2, diagnostic score (DHS) 88.0; best standalone (Gemini 3.1 Pro): 60%, 62.5, 75.7. Llama-4-Scout sensor 56% top-1 vs standalone GPT-OSS-120B 40%.
limits: Table columns read from text extraction; n=50 per cell; simulated patients; needs a knowledge base of symptom likelihoods.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our design: model fills slots, program decides. A direct data point for G5.

source: Kesmen et al. (2026) MoBayes
finding: The gain is architectural, not from extra data: with the knowledge base itself written by the same LLM, gains stay at about 10x lower cost.
numbers: A cheap same-family MoBayes sensor matched the frontier standalone's selective accuracy in both LLM-KB ecosystems at roughly 10x lower per-token cost; the standalone drops sharply on rare diseases from its own world model.
limits: Both knowledge base and patients come from LLM beliefs, so shared bias is possible.
agent_relevance: One elicitation of beliefs into a table, then computation, beats turn-by-turn model reasoning.

source: Kesmen et al. (2026) MoBayes
finding: The stopping threshold trades coverage for accuracy; focusing EIG on the top few suspects helps, but too much focus hurts.
numbers: Threshold sweep (GPT KB, n=50): threshold 0 -> selective accuracy 70, coverage 100; threshold 0.7 -> 100, 40. Focused top-3 EIG: +12 pp top-1 in one passage, 'up to +7 pp' DHS in another (text inconsistent); too strong focus degrades; k=5 slightly worse than k=3.
limits: Appendix ablations; n=50; the two numbers use different metrics.
agent_relevance: Two-phase probe selection: global split first, then discriminate among the top 2-3 suspects. Premature commitment is a stated risk (G1, G6).

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Simulating future answer branches and scoring questions by information gain raised success on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting.
numbers: Average +38.1% relative success over direct prompting across models. GPT-4 (Table 7): Common 49.0 -> 70.9; Things 30.8 -> 36.8; DX 89.4 -> 97.0; MedDG 74.9 -> 87.9; FloDial troubleshooting 43.7 -> 67.3 (7.8 turns).
limits: Simulated patients with LLM answers. Tests are binary questions. Small test sets (DX 104 dialogues, 5 diseases).
agent_relevance: Troubleshooting is the nearest analogue to our diagnosis framing. EIG over simulated futures works with off-the-shelf models.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts
finding: At matched token cost, UoT still beats tree-of-thought, and the uncertainty reward is the active ingredient.
numbers: Swapping the ToT self-evaluation reward for the uncertainty reward adds 5.9% on average. Adapted-ToT at depth 4 (matching UoT depth 3 cost) still underperforms. Averages: vs CoT-SC +33.8%, vs Reflexion +29.9%, vs Adapted-ToT +12.4%.
limits: Cost parity measured in GPT-4 tokens only. Gains differ by model: Llama3-70B open-source DX 26.0 -> 35.6, MedDG 25.7 -> 50.6.
agent_relevance: Self-evaluation of questions is a poorer score than uncertainty over outcomes. Supports G5 and G7.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts
finding: Gains are uneven and depend on how cleanly each answer rules out hypotheses.
numbers: 20Q Things set (1854 items): GPT-4 only 30.8 -> 36.8; Llama3-70B closed-set Things 15.0 -> 25.0. Authors note an answer like 'I don't have a fever' does not eliminate cleanly.
limits: Soft answers break the clean split assumption.
agent_relevance: Probes need crisp outcomes. For code and ARC the test output is crisp, a favourable regime.

source: Zhang, Lu, Jaitly (2023) Probing the Multi-turn Planning Capabilities of LLMs via 20 Question Games
finding: Un-scaffolded LLMs are weak at choosing questions: even GPT-4 wins only a third to a half of games. Failure modes include early enumeration (guessing items one by one) and repeated questions.
numbers: GPT-4 success 0.31 (Things) and 0.50 (Celebrities), about 17.5 turns. GPT-3.5 0.28/0.27; Claude-2 0.21/0.31; Vicuna 7B 0.09/0.06. 30 items x 5 runs. Behaviour cloning of a stronger model: over 70% gain for Vicuna 7B. RL from game-play: 7B Things 0.26.
limits: Strict exact-match scoring. 30 items per set. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Baseline for no scaffold. Early enumeration is the wrong-probe failure to block in S7 (do not guess before the survivor set is small).

source: Zhang, Lu, Jaitly (2023) Probing the Multi-turn Planning Capabilities of LLMs via 20 Question Games
finding: The authors state that GPT-4 outperforms human players by a large margin on this game.
numbers: Model numbers are in c23; the human comparison appears in the abstract and I did not locate human figures.
quote: strong LLMs like GPT-4 outperform human players by a large margin
limits: Human baseline details not verified.
agent_relevance: Models can beat unaided humans at question efficiency, so the human benchmark is not the ceiling.

source: Tajwar et al. (2025) Training a Generally Curious Agent (PAPRIKA)
finding: Fine-tuning on synthetic multi-turn tasks (20 Questions, Wordle, Mastermind, Battleship, Minesweeper and others) teaches in-context exploration with fewer turns to solve.
numbers: Curriculum over easy/medium/hard 20Q topics gave +1.4% and +3.3% over uniform sampling. Train split 477 easy, 726 medium, 296 hard topics. Trained agent used fewer average turns.
limits: Only part of the results read; full transfer table not read. Training-based, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Probe choice can be learned, but we cannot train. Its task list is a good pool of test environments for our scaffold.

source: Ding et al. (2026) Whom to Query for What: Adaptive Group Elicitation via Multi-Turn LLM Interactions
finding: LLM-scored EIG for question choice plus graph propagation to impute missing answers improves prediction under a query budget. Greedy EIG selection beats random.
numbers: Over 12% relative gain on CES at a 10% respondent budget: 17.1% in round 1 down to 12.6% by round 4 vs strongest baseline. Greedy selection has a near-optimal bound (constant factor, submodular case).
limits: Survey setting, not diagnosis. LLM imputation alone was unreliable (Meta-Greedy-Imp no better than Meta-Greedy).
agent_relevance: Cost-weighted selection under a hard budget has theory behind greedy choice.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu, van der Schaar (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Treats clarifying-question choice as Bayesian experimental design; choosing by estimated EIG beats methods that reason only in question space.
numbers: Abstract page only; no numbers read.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as c01: score candidate questions by how they split the solutions.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov, Ellis (2023) Active Preference Inference using Language Models and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: Early LLM loop that picks questions by expected entropy reduction and expected model change; beat same-LLM baselines on a web-shopping preference task with fewer interactions.
numbers: Abstract seen via search only; no numbers.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Earliest example of EIG inside an LLM loop.

source: de Kleer and Williams (1987) Diagnosing multiple faults (GDE)
finding: Classic system: keep candidate fault sets with probabilities and choose the next measurement that minimises expected entropy of the candidate distribution (one-step lookahead).
numbers: Not read this session; described from background knowledge, no numbers.
limits: Not opened; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: The origin of our S7 probe rule. Half-split is the equal-probability, two-outcome case.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation (cited by BED-LLM and ASIG)
finding: Cited in c01 and c15: LLMs often fail to notice when they need more information and fail to gather it in multi-turn use.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Seen only as a citation.
agent_relevance: Motivation for putting the 'do I need a probe' decision in code, not the model.
